overview: This unit examines how functions map subsets to images (Bilder) and form preimages (Urbilder), and how injectivity (Injektivität) and surjectivity (Surjektivität) determine the equalities that hold. Function values induce equivalence classes (Äquivalenzklassen); injections (Injektionen) and bijections (Bijektionen) compare the sizes of sets. Cantor's pairing function (Cantorsche Paarungsfunktion) shows that ℕ, ℤ, and ℚ are countable (abzählbar), while Cantor's diagonal argument proves that power sets and ℝ are uncountable (überabzählbar).

entries.term: Notation for number sets (Zahlmengen) and finite index sets (endliche Indexmengen)
entries.short: ℕ denotes the positive natural numbers, ℕ₀ also includes 0, and [n] denotes {1,…,n}.
entries.explanation: We have ℕ={1,2,3,…} and ℕ₀={0,1,2,…}. For n∈ℕ₀, [n]={1,…,n}; in particular, [0]=∅. Thus the cardinality (Kardinalität) of a finite set with n elements can be written as |A|=|[n]|=n.
pitfalls: In these lecture notes, ℕ does not include 0.
entries.heading: 0. Notation

entries.term: Power set (Potenzmenge), function set (Funktionsmenge), and Cartesian product (kartesisches Produkt)
entries.short: 𝒫(A)=2^A is the set of all subsets of A, B^A is the set of all functions A→B, and A×B is the Cartesian product.
entries.explanation: The power set is 𝒫(A)={X | X⊆A}; it is also the set of functions A→{0,1}. The function set B^A contains all functions with domain A and codomain B. The Cartesian product A×B consists of the ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B; also, im(f)=f(A) denotes the image of f.
entries.example: For A={x,y}, we have 𝒫(A)={∅,{x},{y},{x,y}}.
pitfalls: 2^A denotes a power set, not an ordinary numerical power.
The converse relation fᵀ is not the preimage operation f⁻¹ on subsets.
entries.heading: 0. Notation

entries.short: The image collects the function values of elements in a subset, while the preimage collects all elements whose function values lie in a target subset.
entries.explanation: For f:A→B and X⊆A, f(X)={f(a) | a∈X}; the image of the function is im(f)=f(A). For Y⊆B, f⁻¹(Y)={a∈A | f(a)∈Y}. For a single b∈B, f⁻¹(b) is often used as shorthand for f⁻¹({b}); the preimage operation is defined for every function, whereas an inverse function exists only for a bijection.
pitfalls: A preimage can be empty or contain several elements.
The preimage of a set is not an inverse function and need not be a single element.
entries.heading: 1.1 Einzelne Elemente vs. Mengen

entries.short: Taking a preimage after mapping forward can add elements, whereas mapping forward after taking a preimage gives exactly the reachable part of the target set.
entries.explanation: For X⊆A and Y⊆B, we have f⁻¹(B)=A, X⊆f⁻¹(f(X)), and f(f⁻¹(Y))=Y∩im(f)⊆Y. Also, f(X)⊆Y if and only if X⊆f⁻¹(Y). Extra elements in the first expression arise when different elements have the same function value; the second expression omits elements of Y that are not reached.
pitfalls: In general, neither f⁻¹(f(X))=X nor f(f⁻¹(Y))=Y holds.
entries.heading: 1.2 Bild und Urbild hintereinander

entries.term: Monotonicity (Monotonie) and set operations under functions
entries.short: Images and preimages are monotone, but preimages always preserve unions, intersections, and differences as equalities.
entries.explanation: If X⊆X′, then f(X)⊆f(X′), and if Y⊆Y′, then f⁻¹(Y)⊆f⁻¹(Y′). Images preserve unions as equalities; for intersections, in general f(X∩X′)⊆f(X)∩f(X′), and for differences, f(X\X′)⊇f(X)\f(X′). Preimages preserve unions, intersections, and differences as equalities.
entries.example: If f(1)=f(5)=r, X={1}, and X′={5}, then f(X∩X′)=∅, but f(X)∩f(X′)={r}.
pitfalls: The inclusion for image differences points in the direction f(X)\f(X′)⊆f(X\X′).
Image equalities for intersections and differences do not hold for every function.
entries.heading: 1.3 Monotonie und Mengenoperationen

entries.short: A function is surjective if every element of its codomain has at least one preimage.
entries.explanation: For f:A→B, f is surjective if and only if f(A)=B. Equivalently, f(f⁻¹(Y))=Y for every subset Y⊆B. In particular, every b∈B is reached by at least one a∈A; a target value may have several preimages.
entries.example: f:ℤ→ℕ₀ with f(n)=|n| is surjective, because every k∈ℕ₀ is reached as f(k).
pitfalls: Surjectivity depends on the specified codomain.
Surjectivity does not require every target object to have exactly one preimage.
entries.heading: 2.1 Surjektivität

entries.short: A function is injective if distinct elements of its domain have distinct function values.
entries.explanation: For f:A→B, injectivity means that f(a)=f(a′) always implies a=a′. Equivalently, f⁻¹(f(X))=X for every X⊆A. Another equivalent condition is that f preserves intersections and differences of subsets exactly; in particular, f(A\X)=f(A)\f(X).
entries.example: f:ℤ→ℤ with f(n)=2n is injective, since 2n=2m forces n=m.
pitfalls: Injectivity requires at most one preimage per target value; it does not require every target value to be reached.
The equality f⁻¹(f(X))=X must hold for every X⊆A.
entries.heading: 2.2 Injektivität

entries.short: A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
entries.explanation: A bijective function f:A→B reaches every element of B exactly once. It has an inverse function f⁻¹:B→A if and only if it is bijective. Equivalently, f(A\X)=B\f(X) for every X⊆A; a bijection also shows that A and B have the same cardinality.
entries.example: f:ℤ→2ℤ with f(n)=2n is bijective when 2ℤ denotes the even integers.
pitfalls: An injection need not be surjective, and a surjection need not be injective.
The equality f(A\X)=B\f(X) holds for every X if and only if f is bijective.
entries.heading: 2.3 Bijektivität

entries.short: A function declares two elements of its domain equivalent when they have the same function value.
entries.explanation: Every function f:A→B induces the relation a≡f a′ if and only if f(a)=f(a′) on A. It is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, and is therefore an equivalence relation. The class of an element is [a]f=f⁻¹({f(a)}), the set of all elements with the same function value.
entries.example: For f:ℤ→ℕ₀ with f(n)=|n|, we have 2≡f−2, but 2 is not equivalent to 3.
pitfalls: The relation compares function values; equivalent elements need not be equal.
related: Equivalence class and quotient of a function
entries.heading: 3. Funktionen erzeugen Äquivalenzrelationen (Folie 139)

entries.term: Equivalence class and quotient of a function (Äquivalenzklasse und Quotient einer Funktion)
entries.short: The equivalence class of an element contains all elements with the same function value, and the quotient consists of these classes.
entries.explanation: For the relation induced by f:A→B, we have [a]f=f⁻¹({f(a)}). The quotient A/≡f={ [a]f | a∈A } consists exactly of the nonempty preimages of function values that are reached. These classes partition A into disjoint groups, each of which corresponds to exactly one element of im(f).
entries.example: If f(1)=f(5)=r and f(2)=f(4)=g, then {1,5} and {2,4} are two equivalence classes.
pitfalls: Elements of B that are not reached do not produce a class.
Elements of the quotient are classes, not the original individual elements.
entries.heading: 3. Funktionen erzeugen Äquivalenzrelationen (Folie 139)

entries.term: Factorization of a function through the quotient (Faktorisierung einer Funktion über den Quotienten)
entries.short: Every function can be written as a surjective map onto its equivalence classes followed by an injective map into its image.
entries.explanation: Define π:A→A/≡f by π(a)=[a]f and f̃:A/≡f→B by f̃([a]f)=f(a). The map f̃ is well-defined and injective, and f=f̃∘π. The projection π is surjective; if f is injective, all classes are singletons, and if f is surjective, f̃ is bijective.
entries.example: For f(n)=|n|, π groups the numbers n and −n; f̃ assigns their common absolute value to each class.
pitfalls: The value f̃([a]f) is independent of the representative, since all elements of a class have the same function value.
related: Equivalence class and quotient of a function
entries.heading: 3. Funktionen erzeugen Äquivalenzrelationen (Folie 139)

entries.short: |A|≤|B| means that an injection A→B exists, and |A|=|B| means that a bijection A→B exists.
entries.explanation: Cardinality compares the sizes of sets regardless of whether they contain the same elements. We have |A|≤|B| if and only if there is an injective function A→B, and |A|=|B| if and only if there is a bijective function A→B. |A|<|B| means |A|≤|B| and |A|≠|B|; for finite sets, |A|=n means that A is in bijection with [n].
entries.example: The injection {a,b}→{1,2,3} with a↦1 and b↦2 shows that |{a,b}|≤|{1,2,3}|.
pitfalls: A non-surjective injection alone does not prove that the sets have different cardinalities.
Having the same cardinality means that a bijection exists, not that the sets are identical.
entries.heading: 4.1 Definition

entries.short: Inclusions and compositions of injections or bijections give basic cardinality comparisons.
entries.explanation: From A⊆B, the inclusion map gives |A|≤|B|. The identity function shows |A|≤|A| and |A|=|A|; a bijection A→B shows both cardinality inequalities. Injections can be composed, so |A|≤|B| and |B|≤|C| together imply |A|≤|C|; for the same reason, having the same cardinality is transitive.
entries.example: An injection A→B and an injection B→C compose to give an injection A→C.
pitfalls: A proper subset of an infinite set need not have smaller cardinality.
entries.heading: 4.2 Grundregeln

entries.short: If there are injections in both directions between two sets, then there is a bijection between them.
entries.explanation: The theorem states that |A|=|B| if and only if |A|≤|B| and |B|≤|A|. For the nontrivial direction, an injection A→B and an injection B→A suffice to conclude that there is a bijection A→B. The two injections need not be inverses of each other.
entries.example: Given injections A→B and B→A, the theorem allows us to conclude that |A|=|B|.
pitfalls: A single injection does not prove that two sets have the same cardinality.
The two injections need not be inverses of each other.
entries.heading: 4.3 Satz von Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder (CBS)

entries.term: Countability, countably infinite, and uncountable (Abzählbarkeit, abzählbar unendlich und überabzählbar)
entries.short: A set is countable if it can be mapped injectively into ℕ, and countably infinite if it has the same cardinality as ℕ.
entries.explanation: Countability means |A|≤|ℕ| and includes finite sets. Countably infinite means |A|=|ℕ|, that is, there is a bijection with the positive natural numbers. A set is uncountable if it is not countable; every countable set is finite or countably infinite.
entries.example: The positive even numbers form a countably infinite set, even though they are a proper subset of ℕ.
pitfalls: Countable does not mean exclusively countably infinite.
An enumeration need not be computable by an algorithm.
related: Equipotence of ℕ and the positive even numbers
entries.heading: 5. Abzählbare Mengen (Folie 143, PDF 183–184)

entries.term: Equipotence of ℕ and the positive even numbers (Gleichmächtigkeit von ℕ und den positiven geraden Zahlen)
entries.short: The positive natural numbers and the positive even numbers have the same cardinality, although the even numbers form a proper subset.
entries.explanation: The function f:ℕ→2ℕ with f(n)=2n is bijective, where 2ℕ={2,4,6,…}. Its inverse function assigns each positive even number m the value m/2. Hence |ℕ|=|2ℕ|, and this example shows that a proper subset of an infinite set can have the same cardinality as the whole set.
pitfalls: Here 2ℕ denotes the positive even numbers, not 2^ℕ or a power set.
entries.heading: 5.1 Natürliche Zahlen und gerade Zahlen

entries.short: The integers are countably infinite because they can be mapped bijectively to the positive natural numbers.
entries.explanation: A bijection f:ℤ→ℕ is given by f(z)=2z+1 for z≥0 and f(z)=−2z for z<0. Nonnegative numbers map to positive odd numbers, and negative numbers map to positive even numbers. These sets are disjoint and together form ℕ, so |ℤ|=|ℕ|; ℕ₀ also has the same cardinality as ℕ.
pitfalls: The map must include both negative and nonnegative numbers without omissions.
entries.heading: 5.2 Ganze Zahlen

entries.term: Every countable set is finite or countably infinite
entries.short: A set that can be mapped injectively into ℕ is either finite or has the same cardinality as ℕ.
entries.explanation: Let f:A→ℕ be injective. If f(A) is bounded, it is finite and, by injectivity, A is finite as well. If f(A) is unbounded, its values can be selected in increasing order by choosing the least value not yet chosen each time. The unique preimages of these values give an enumeration without repetition and hence a bijection ℕ→A.
entries.example: The set of square numbers is an infinite subset of ℕ and is therefore countably infinite.
pitfalls: An unbounded image f(A)⊆ℕ need not be all of ℕ.
entries.heading: 5.3 Jede abzählbare Menge ist endlich oder abzählbar unendlich

entries.short: Cantor's pairing function assigns a unique positive natural number to each pair of positive natural numbers.
entries.explanation: For n,m∈ℕ, p(n,m)=m+((n+m−1)(n+m−2))/2. Pairs with the same sum n+m lie on the same finite diagonal; the formula counts the pairs on earlier diagonals, then the position m on the current diagonal. The diagonals receive consecutive, disjoint blocks of numbers, so p is bijective and ℕ×ℕ is countable.
pitfalls: The formula uses positive natural-number coordinates n,m≥1.
The pairing function enumerates diagonals; Cantor's diagonal argument refutes a purported complete list.
entries.heading: 6.1 Warum ist sogar $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ abzählbar?

entries.term: Countability of finite tuples of natural numbers
entries.short: For every fixed finite length, tuples of natural numbers are countable, and the set of all finite nonempty tuples is also countable.
entries.explanation: Repeated application of Cantor's pairing function shows |ℕᵏ|=|ℕ| for every fixed k∈ℕ. The union of all sets ℕᵏ for k∈ℕ is also countable. An alternative encoding of (n₁,…,nₖ) is 2ⁿ¹3ⁿ²⋯pₖⁿᵏ; prime factorization reconstructs the entries and tuple length, and the empty tuple can be encoded separately by 1.
entries.example: The tuple (2,1) is encoded by 2²·3¹=12.
pitfalls: The statement concerns finite tuples, not all infinite sequences of natural numbers.
entries.heading: 6.2 Endliche Tupel beliebiger Länge

entries.short: The rational numbers are countable because they can be encoded injectively using integer numerators and positive denominators.
entries.explanation: Every rational number can be represented as z/m with z∈ℤ and m∈ℕ. The fully reduced fraction with positive denominator is unique, including 0=0/1, so this gives an injection ℚ→ℤ×ℕ. Together with an injection ℕ→ℚ and the countability of ℤ×ℕ, Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder gives |ℚ|=|ℕ|.
entries.example: The fully reduced fraction for −6/8 is −3/4.
pitfalls: Without reduction, the same rational number would have multiple representations.
The density of ℚ in ℝ does not mean that ℚ is uncountable.
entries.heading: 6.3 Warum $\mathbb Q$ abzählbar ist

entries.short: The set of all finite binary words is countably infinite.
entries.explanation: The set of all finite binary words is {0,1}*=⋃ₖ∈ℕ₀ {0,1}ᵏ. Prefix each word with a leading 1 and read the result as a binary number to obtain a bijection with the positive natural numbers. Every positive number has a unique binary representation that begins with 1.
entries.example: The empty word becomes 1, the word 0 becomes 10, and the word 1 becomes 11.
pitfalls: The asterisk denotes words of arbitrary finite length, not infinite bit sequences.
entries.heading: 6.4 Endliche Wörter

entries.short: For every set A, its power set has strictly greater cardinality than A.
entries.explanation: The theorem states |A|<|𝒫(A)|=|2^A|. The map a↦{a} is an injection A→𝒫(A), so first we have |A|≤|𝒫(A)|. The diagonal argument shows that no function A→𝒫(A) can be surjective, so in particular no bijection exists; together these give the strict inequality.
entries.example: For A=ℕ, we have |ℕ|<|𝒫(ℕ)|.
pitfalls: The theorem also holds for infinite sets.
The power set contains all subsets, not ordinary numerical powers.
entries.heading: 7. Satz von Cantor (Folie 144, PDF 185–186)

entries.term: Injection into the power set (Injektion in die Potenzmenge)
entries.short: The map that sends each element to its singleton subset is an injection A→𝒫(A).
entries.explanation: Define f:A→𝒫(A) by f(a)={a}. From f(a)=f(b), we get {a}={b} and hence a=b, so f is injective. Therefore |A|≤|𝒫(A)|; this map gives the first part of the proof of Cantor's theorem.
entries.example: For A={x,y}, we have f(x)={x} and f(y)={y}.
pitfalls: The injection does not show that every element of the power set is a singleton.
related: Power set, function set, and Cartesian product
entries.heading: 7.1 Beweis, Teil 1: Injektion

entries.short: For g:A→𝒫(A), the diagonal set consists exactly of the elements that do not belong to their assigned subset.
entries.explanation: Define D={a∈A | a∉g(a)}; since D⊆A, we have D∈𝒫(A). Suppose g is surjective. Then there is d∈A such that g(d)=D. It follows that d∈D if and only if d∉g(d), which is equivalent to d∉D, a contradiction.
entries.example: For each a, D includes a if and only if a is not contained in g(a).
pitfalls: The contradiction refutes the assumed surjectivity of g, not the existence of D.
entries.heading: 7.2 Beweis, Teil 2: Diagonalargument

entries.short: To refute a purported complete list, construct an object that differs from every listed entry at a position specific to that entry.
entries.explanation: Suppose g:A→𝒫(A) is surjective, and form D={a∈A | a∉g(a)}. Surjectivity would give some d with g(d)=D, but D differs from g(d) precisely at d, a contradiction. For a list of bit sequences, the same idea works by flipping the n-th bit of the n-th row.
entries.example: From a list of bit sequences, form a new sequence by negating each diagonal bit.
pitfalls: Do not confuse this with Cantor's pairing function, which enumerates the diagonals of a number grid.
The surjectivity assumption is needed to obtain an index d with g(d)=D.
entries.heading: 7.3 Was genau ist an der Konstruktion so clever?

entries.term: Diagonal argument as a table (Diagonalargument als Tabelle)
entries.short: For a tabular listing of subsets, form a new bit sequence by negating each diagonal bit.
entries.explanation: Represent a purported list g(1),g(2),… of subsets of ℕ as rows, where a 1 in column n means that n belongs to the subset. Set dₙ=1−g(n)ₙ, the opposite of the n-th bit in the n-th row. The new sequence differs from row n at position n and therefore cannot appear in any row.
entries.example: If the diagonal is 0,1,0,0,…, the negated diagonal is 1,0,1,1,….
pitfalls: The new sequence only needs to differ from each row at its diagonal position.
entries.heading: 7.4 Diagonalargument als Tabelle für $A=\mathbb N$

entries.short: Every subset of ℕ corresponds to exactly one infinite bit sequence whose bits indicate membership of the natural numbers.
entries.explanation: For S⊆ℕ, the characteristic function χS:ℕ→{0,1} is defined by χS(n)=1 for n∈S and χS(n)=0 for n∉S. It gives a bijection between 𝒫(ℕ) and {0,1}^ℕ, the set of infinite bit sequences. Conversely, every bit sequence determines the subset of positions at which a 1 occurs.
entries.example: The subset {1,3} corresponds to the sequence 1,0,1,0,0,….
pitfalls: {0,1}^ℕ contains infinite sequences; {0,1}* contains only finite words.
related: Power set, function set, and Cartesian product
entries.heading: 8.1 Endliche vs. unendliche Bitfolgen

entries.term: Different cardinalities of finite and infinite bit sequences
entries.short: Finite binary words are countable, whereas infinite bit sequences are uncountable.
entries.explanation: We have |{0,1}*|=|ℕ|, because all finite words can be encoded by natural numbers. The bijection via characteristic functions gives |{0,1}^ℕ|=|𝒫(ℕ)|. By Cantor's theorem, |ℕ|<|𝒫(ℕ)|, so infinite bit sequences are uncountable.
entries.example: All finite words can be listed, but a purported list of all infinite bit sequences can be refuted by diagonalization.
pitfalls: Having finitely many bit sequences of each fixed length does not make the set of all infinite sequences countable.
entries.heading: 8.1 Endliche vs. unendliche Bitfolgen

entries.term: Cardinality of infinite bit sequences and the interval [0,1]
entries.short: The set of infinite bit sequences and the interval [0,1] have the same cardinality.
entries.explanation: A bit sequence b₁b₂… can be read as the sum ∑ₙ₌₁∞ bₙ/2ⁿ, but this assignment is not injective because of duplicate binary representations. An injection [0,1]→{0,1}^ℕ is obtained using unique canonical binary representations; for 1, choose the sequence 111… . In the other direction, b↦∑ₙ₌₁∞2bₙ/3ⁿ is injective, because the difference at the first position where the sequences differ is greater than the sum of all possible later contributions that could offset it. Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder gives the equality of cardinalities.
entries.example: The sequence 1,0,1,… is read as the binary expansion 0,101…₂.
pitfalls: A real number can have more than one binary expansion.
The injection from bit sequences into [0,1] uses a ternary encoding.
entries.heading: 8.2 Unendliche Bitfolgen und das Intervall $[0,1]$

entries.term: Equipotence of ℝ and (0,1) (Gleichmächtigkeit von ℝ und (0,1))
entries.short: A bijection maps the real numbers to the open interval (0,1), so the two sets have the same cardinality.
entries.explanation: The function f:ℝ→(0,1), f(x)=1/(1+2⁻ˣ), is strictly increasing and has inverse function f⁻¹(y)=log₂(y/(1−y)). Its limits as x→−∞ and x→+∞ are 0 and 1; no finite x maps to an endpoint. Since (0,1)⊆[0,1]⊆ℝ, the inclusions and Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder imply that all three sets have the same cardinality.
pitfalls: The codomain is (0,1); the endpoints 0 and 1 are not attained.
related: Cardinality of infinite bit sequences and the interval [0,1]
entries.heading: 8.3 Warum ein kleines Intervall genauso mächtig wie ganz $\mathbb R$ ist

entries.short: The real numbers are uncountable because their cardinality equals that of the power set of ℕ.
entries.explanation: Cantor's theorem gives |ℕ|<|𝒫(ℕ)|. Characteristic functions show that 𝒫(ℕ) has the same cardinality as the infinite bit sequences; these have the same cardinality as [0,1], and [0,1] has the same cardinality as ℝ. Thus |ℕ|<|ℝ|, so ℝ is uncountable; together with the countability of ℚ, this gives |ℚ|<|ℝ|.
pitfalls: Density or the ordering of a set alone says nothing about its cardinality.
related: Different cardinalities of finite and infinite bit sequences
entries.heading: 8.4 Gesamtergebnis: $\mathbb R$ ist überabzählbar

entries.short: There are real numbers that no program can compute to arbitrary precision by means of approximations.
entries.explanation: Programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet and are therefore at most countable in number. Each program that computes a real number through arbitrarily precise approximations determines at most one such number. Since ℝ is uncountable, programs cannot compute all real numbers; countability alone also does not guarantee that a program can enumerate the elements of a set.
entries.example: There are at most countably many programs, but uncountably many real numbers.
pitfalls: Countability is a statement about the size of a set, not automatically about the algorithmic computability of its elements.
entries.heading: 8.5 Kurzer Informatikbezug (direkt anschließende Bemerkung auf Folie 145)
